specAnchors.text: be able to calculate mean bond enthalpies from enthalpy changes of reaction
understand the terms ‘bond enthalpy’ and ‘mean bond enthalpy’, and be able to use bond enthalpies to calculate enthalpy changes, understanding the limitations of this method

primer.text: Breaking a bond costs energy; making one pays it back. The balance between the two accounts is the overall enthalpy change. This note defines mean bond enthalpy, works the broken-minus-formed equation on real reactions, and derives a bond enthalpy from an experimental enthalpy change, then explains why the averages can mislead.

modules.title: The bond ledger: breaking pays, forming earns
modules.opening: Every reaction is a bond transaction: energy is paid in to break bonds and earned back when new bonds form. The overall enthalpy change is simply the ledger balance - total break costs minus total formation earnings.
keyPoints: Breaking bonds requires energy from the surroundings, so bond breaking is endothermic.
Forming bonds releases energy to the surroundings, so bond formation is exothermic.
The overall enthalpy change equals the total energy to break bonds minus the total energy released forming bonds.
Bond enthalpies apply to gases - all species must be gaseous for the ledger to work.
A negative balance means the formation earnings outweighed the break costs: exothermic.

low.restatement: Add up what it costs to snap every bond broken, add up what is earned making every new bond, and subtract earnings from costs - the balance is the reaction's enthalpy change.
low.analogy: Demolition and construction: pay the wreckers, collect from the builders, and the net spend is the enthalpy change.
low.examPointer: Write the master equation in symbols first - sum(broken) minus sum(formed) - then substitute numbers; sign errors cluster in word-first approaches.

medium.restatement: The gas-phase restriction matters because tabulated bond enthalpies are measured between free gaseous atoms; solutions and solids carry extra intermolecular terms the ledger cannot see.
medium.analogy: The ledger only audits the molecule's own accounts, not its neighbourhood fees - liquids and solids charge neighbourhood fees.
medium.examPointer: When a question gives aqueous species, expect the answer to explain why bond-enthalpy arithmetic is unreliable there.

modules.title: Mean bond enthalpy and its limits
modules.opening: Tabulated bond enthalpies are averages: the C-H value summarises methane's four bonds, ethane's six, and every other environment into one number. Averages are useful and imprecise - knowing which is which separates good answers from great ones.
keyPoints: A mean bond enthalpy averages a bond's dissociation energy across many compounds.
Methane's mean C-H enthalpy is a quarter of its total atomisation enthalpy: four identical bonds share the bill.
The average hides environment: a C-H bond costs more to break in some molecules than in others.
Averages are measured in the gas phase, so solution calculations inherit systematic error.
Mean values give approximate enthalpy changes - data-book values beat them when available.

low.restatement: One C-H number serves every molecule because it averages them all: methane's four equal bonds split their total bill into four equal shares.
low.analogy: A menu's 'average meal price' - no actual meal costs exactly that, but it predicts the bill reasonably.
low.examPointer: Define mean bond enthalpy with the word 'average' or 'mean' and the phrase 'across a range of compounds' - precision earns the mark.

medium.restatement: The averaging is the limitation's root: since each specific bond's true strength depends on its molecular neighbourhood, cycle calculations built on means drift from measured values, and the drift grows with structural complexity.
medium.analogy: Averages are shoe sizes: close enough to walk in, wrong for the marathon.
medium.examPointer: Name at least two limitations (averaging, gas phase) when asked - single-limitation answers score half.

modules.title: Calculations: pricing reactions and deriving bonds
modules.opening: Two calculation directions share one ledger: price a reaction from tabulated bonds (broken minus formed), or solve the ledger backwards to derive a bond enthalpy from a measured reaction enthalpy. Both are bookkeeping - the second just hides one number.
keyPoints: The forward calculation prices a reaction: sum the bonds broken, sum the bonds formed, subtract.
Hydrogen chloride synthesis works as (+436 + 242) - 2(431) = -184 kJ mol^-1.
The reverse direction solves for an unknown bond enthalpy from a measured enthalpy change.
Ammonia's ledger derives the mean N-H bond: broken 2252, formed 2344, so each N-H costs 2344/6.
Both directions assume gaseous species and mean bond values - approximations to declare.

low.restatement: List every bond broken on the left, every bond formed on the right, multiply by their tabulated values, and subtract formed from broken - or hide one value and solve for it.
low.analogy: A receipt with one missing price: total the known lines, subtract from the bill, and the missing line prices itself.
low.examPointer: Count bonds carefully - diatomic products like HCl appear twice per equation unit, so their bond value is multiplied by two.

medium.restatement: The reverse derivation treats the ledger as an equation in one unknown: measured change plus total formed equals total broken, so isolating the unknown bond delivers the 6.10 skill of extracting mean bond enthalpies from experimental data.
medium.analogy: Auditing backwards: the bank statement (measured change) reveals the hidden transaction (the unknown bond) once every other line is priced.
medium.examPointer: Declare the approximations in writing: mean values and gas-phase assumptions - the qualification is part of the marking scheme.

glossary.definition: The energy required to break one mole of a named bond in gaseous molecules.
The average bond dissociation energy for a bond type across a range of compounds.
The conversion of a substance into free gaseous atoms.

workedExample.prompt: Using mean bond enthalpies H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 242 and H-Cl = 431 kJ mol^-1, calculate the enthalpy change of H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g).
steps: Bonds broken: one H-H and one Cl-Cl, costing 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.
Bonds formed: two H-Cl bonds, earning 2 x 431 = 862 kJ.
The negative balance confirms formation outearned breaking.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The enthalpy change is -184 kJ mol^-1 (exothermic).
